listenings.text: Okay, you asked what I actually think, so here it is, with all the hedging included. I am not entirely sure, but I would argue that the exam measures the wrong thing. It must measure something, obviously, or the results would be random, and they are not. What I would say is that it cannot measure the thing everybody claims it measures, because a test that lasts one morning cannot see whether somebody can work for six years. That is speculation on my part. I have no data. But notice what I am not saying. I am not saying it should be abolished. I would not rule out that it is the least bad system anybody has managed to build. Those are two different claims, and people collapse them into one all the time.

The thing people get wrong about confidence in argument is that they treat it as volume. It is not volume. It is calibration. A speaker who says every sentence with the same certainty is not confident, he is just loud, and an audience works that out in about ninety seconds. What actually persuades is a speaker who marks the difference. This I am sure of. This I am fairly sure of. This is a guess and I will tell you it is a guess. Once you do that, the strong claims land, because they are no longer competing with the weak ones. And here is the part my students never believe until they try it. Saying I am not certain about this does not cost you authority. It buys you the authority you need for the next sentence.

Voting is compulsory in about twenty countries and optional in most of the rest, and the argument between them is older than any of us. In one column, the countries that compel say a democracy in which only the motivated vote is not a democracy, it is a survey of the motivated. In the other, the countries that do not say an obligation to participate is a contradiction in terms. What is interesting is what the numbers actually show. Turnout in compulsory systems is higher, which surprises nobody. But the size of the gap is smaller than most people assume, and in several countries the fine is so low that the obligation is effectively a suggestion with paperwork. So before you take a side, it is worth asking which version of compulsory you are actually arguing about.
